newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia cenbank official sees moderate '97 growth.
newsitem.headline: Colombia cenbank official sees moderate '97 growth.

text.p: A senior central bank official said he sees Colombia's gross domestic product growing by a moderate 2.5 to 3.0 percent this year, but he cautioned the government against relying on further cuts in interest rates to spur growth.
Salomon Kalmanovitz, a member of the policy-making board of directors of the Banco de la Republica, gave his growth forecast in a rare interview with Bogota's respected El Espectador newspaper.

"If production begins to recover, and the second quarter was better than the first, I think gross domestic product should grow by between 2.5 and three percent this year," Kalmanovitz told the newspaper.
Colombia's GDP fell by 1.22 percent in the first quarter, plunging from a 0.1 percent drop in the final quarter of 1996.

Government officials have insisted that growth as high as 3.5 percent is still possible this year, thanks to an expected surge in oil and coffee revenues, but they have also stressed the need for a further drop in domestic interest rates to make this possible.

The central bank cut its benchmark 90-day interest rate by one percentage point to 23 percent in May. But Kalmanovitz said there would be no further easing of monetary policy unless inflationary pressures on the economy subsided.
"We know that the government is very anxious that something be done, but we can't act irresponsibly," he said. "If inflation continues rising, there will be no new reduction in interest rates."
The National Statistics Department is due to release consumer price index figures for June on Wednesday. The index is running at a cumulative 9.94 percent for the first five months of the year.
The influential National Association of Financial Institutions predicted in a report issued Monday that the central bank's 18 percent inflation target for the entire year was unlikely to be met.

In his interview with El Espectador, Kalmanovitz said there were already signs of an economic recovery and stressed his belief that the manufacturing sector had bottomed out after seeing output fall in the first half.
Real interest rates are currently running at about 4-5 percent and the central bank clearly believes there is no need to cut them further, unless economic conditions worsen significantly.
GDP growth as low as 2.5 percent this year would be little to boast about by Colombian standards, and it would be among the lowest of any major country in the region in 1997.
Colombia's gross domestic product grew by just two percent last year, down from a 3.7 percent annual average since 1980 and from bubbling growth of 4.6 percent in January-March 1996.

The government has said repeatedly that efforts to break Colombia's long dependency on drug dollars -- and its crackdown on the Cali cartel -- helped spark the recession the country slid into in the first quarter of 1997.
But Kalmanovitz said a minimum of $2.5 billion in drug money was still being laundered in Colombia annually.
